ALTER DATABASE [culprit_demo] SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE;

An escalation happens when one statement takes about 5,000 locks on one index: SQL Server swaps them for a single lock on the whole table, and every other session that writes to support\_tickets, or reads it without row versioning, waits until that statement's transaction ends. SQL Server doesn't record which statement it was, and none of the statements in the query history writes to support\_tickets. A read can escalate too: under read committed it gives each row lock up as it moves on, but it keeps them until the statement ends when its plan prefetches its key lookups, under a locking hint (HOLDLOCK, UPDLOCK), or in a REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE transaction, and one that reads thousands of rows that way takes enough to escalate. The reads of it are listed below, most rows a run first; the one to look for reads thousands of rows in one run while it keeps its locks.

- Escalations since SQL Server started: **5**

**Query `10`** · 2% of database time · 4.0K runs over the last 5 hours · 1.4 ms on average

```sql

```

**Fix.** Start the event session below (culprit\_lock\_escalation) to learn which statement escalates: it keeps each escalation with its statement, in memory, at almost no cost. If it is a read, it escalates because it keeps its row locks until it ends: READ\_COMMITTED\_SNAPSHOT lets reads under read committed take no row locks at all (it changes what readers see and uses tempdb, so test it first); or read fewer rows a run, so it stays under the 5,000 locks that escalate. If it is a statement outside the query history that changes many rows at once (a job, a migration, maintenance), change it into a loop over at most 1,000 rows at a time, each its own statement.

```sql

-- It catches them on every table, so another table's finding starts this same session: once is enough.

    CREATE EVENT SESSION culprit_lock_escalation ON SERVER
    ADD EVENT sqlserver.lock_escalation (
        SET collect_statement = 1
        ACTION (sqlserver.sql_text, sqlserver.client_app_name)
        WHERE sqlserver.database_name = N'culprit_demo')
    ADD TARGET package0.ring_buffer
    WITH (STARTUP_STATE = ON);
IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sys.dm_xe_sessions WHERE name = N'culprit_lock_escalation')
    ALTER EVENT SESSION culprit_lock_escalation ON SERVER STATE = START;

-- Then read what it caught
SELECT e.x.value('@timestamp', 'datetime2') AS at_utc,
       OBJECT_NAME(e.x.value('(data[@name="object_id"]/value)[1]', 'int')) AS table_name,
       e.x.value('(data[@name="escalated_lock_count"]/value)[1]', 'int') AS locks,
       e.x.value('(data[@name="statement"]/value)[1]', 'nvarchar(max)') AS statement,
       e.x.value('(action[@name="client_app_name"]/value)[1]', 'nvarchar(256)') AS app

          FROM sys.dm_xe_session_targets t
          JOIN sys.dm_xe_sessions s ON s.address = t.event_session_address
         WHERE s.name = N'culprit_lock_escalation' AND t.target_name = N'ring_buffer') r
 CROSS APPLY r.d.nodes('RingBufferTarget/event') e(x);

-- Once it has caught what you need, stop and remove it: DROP EVENT SESSION culprit_lock_escalation ON SERVER;
```
